title: His wife left him. Villagers thought he was mentally ill. He changed how millions of women live. October 3, 2026.
excerpt: From a doctor who proved himself right decades too late, to an inventor who proved himself right while everyone around him doubted him, October 3's five stories share one thread: being dismissed in the moment didn't make any of these people wrong.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about work that was real before anyone agreed it was real - a fertility breakthrough dismissed by the very government that should have celebrated it, a genetics career built one publication at a time toward a national honor, a business fortune redirected into an engineering school's future, a boat engineered to leave nothing behind but water, and an invention built by a man everyone around him thought had lost his mind.

October 3, 1978: a Kolkata doctor achieved the world's second-ever IVF birth - alone, with homemade equipment

Dr. Subhash Mukhopadhyay achieved India's first IVF birth on October 3, 1978, in Kolkata - the baby, Kanupriya Agarwal, was the world's second IVF baby ever, just 67 days after the UK's Louise Brown. Instead of recognition, a state government committee dismissed his claim and barred him from presenting his work internationally. Professionally isolated, he died in 1981. It took until 2002 - 21 years later - for India's Council of Medical Research to formally recognize his pioneering achievement.

He mapped the genetics behind heart disease. In 2026, the American Heart Association gave him its top research honor

Dr. Pradeep Natarajan was named the 2026 recipient of the American Heart Association's Population Research Prize, to be presented in Chicago on November 8, 2026. Vice President of Global Research at Amgen and a Harvard Medical School professor, he has authored over 330 peer-reviewed publications uncovering the genetic roots of coronary artery disease and advancing polygenic risk scores for earlier detection.

She gave a US engineering school $100 million. They renamed it after her family

In October 2015, Chandrika Tandon and her husband Ranjan Tandon donated $100 million to NYU's School of Engineering, one of the largest gifts by an Indian-American in US history - the school was renamed the NYU Tandon School of Engineering. A former McKinsey partner and founder of Tandon Capital Associates, she later won a 2025 Grammy for Best New Age, Ambient, or Chant Album at age 70.

India just put a passenger boat on the Ganga that runs on hydrogen

India's first indigenous hydrogen fuel cell-powered passenger vessel entered commercial service on the Ganga at Varanasi, built by Cochin Shipyard for the Inland Waterways Authority of India. The 24-metre catamaran, carrying up to 50 passengers, runs on a hybrid system of hydrogen fuel cells, batteries and solar panels, with only water as its emission - part of India's National Green Hydrogen Mission.

His wife left him. Villagers thought he was mentally ill. He changed how millions of women live

Arunachalam Muruganantham, a school dropout from Coimbatore, discovered his newly married wife used rags instead of sanitary pads because branded ones were unaffordable. He spent years self-experimenting - facing social ostracism along the way - before inventing a low-cost sanitary-pad-making machine now installed in over 1,300 villages across 23 Indian states. He received the Padma Shri in 2016 and was named to TIME's 100 Most Influential People in 2014.

Five stories, one thread: a doctor proven right only after his death, a researcher whose decades of publications finally earned a national prize, a philanthropist who turned business success into an institution's future, an engineering team that built a boat to leave nothing behind, and an inventor who kept building while everyone around him assumed he'd lost his mind. None of them were wrong just because they were doubted.
